```{r}
library(ICSNP)
library(poolr)
library(car)
```

### 1. Hotelling's $T^2$ Test for a Mean Vector

(a) Evaluate $T^2$ for testing the null hypothesis $H_0$ : $\mu^T$ = [7, 11].

```{r}
x <- matrix(c(2, 12, 8, 9, 6, 9, 8, 10), nrow=4, ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
x

n <- nrow(x)
p <- ncol(x)

t2 <- HotellingsT2(x, mu = c(7, 11))
t2$statistic
```

(b) Specify the exact distribution of $T^2$ under the null hypothesis for this situation.

    The exact distribution is:

    $\frac{n-p}{p(n-1)}T^2$ \~ $F_{p, n-p}$

    Given n (rows) = 4, p (columns) = 2:

    $\frac{4-2}{2(4-1)}T^2$ = $\frac{T^2}{3}$

    Thus, the exact distribution of $T^2$ under the null hypothesis is:

    $T^2$ \~ $3F_{2, 2}$

(c) Using parts (a) and (b), test $H_0$ at the significance level $\alpha$ = 0.05. What statistical conclusion do you reach?

```{r}
Fstat <- ((n - p) / (p * (n - 1))) * t2$statistic
Fstat

# Critical value
qf(0.95, p, n - p)

# p-value
pf(Fstat, p, n - p, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

With a significance level of $\alpha$ = 0.05, we acquire $F_{0.95,2,2}$ = 19. Since the F-statistic = 1.515152 \< 19 we fail to reject $H_0$ at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

### 2. Simultaneous Confidence Intervals and Regions for Grizzly Bear Body Measurements

```{r}
n <- 61
p <- 6 # variables in order are: Weight, Body Length, Neck, Girth, Head Length, Head Width

xbar <- c(95.52, 164.38, 55.69, 93.39, 17.98, 31.13)

S <- matrix(c(
  3266.46, 1343.97, 731.54, 1175.50, 162.68, 238.37,
  1343.97, 721.91, 324.25, 537.35, 80.17, 117.73,
  731.54, 324.25, 179.28, 281.17, 39.15, 56.80,
  1175.50, 537.35, 281.17, 474.98, 63.73, 94.85,
  162.68, 80.17, 39.15, 63.73, 9.95, 13.88,
  238.37, 117.73, 56.80, 94.85, 13.88, 21.26
), nrow = 6, byrow = TRUE)
```

(a) Obtain the large-sample 95% simultaneous confidence intervals for the six population mean body measurements.

```{r}
critical <- qchisq(0.95, df=6)
critical
margin <- sqrt((critical * diag(S))/n)
margin

lwr_bound <- xbar - margin
upr_bound <- xbar + margin

cbind(lwr_bound, upr_bound)
```

(b) Obtain the large-sample 95% simultaneous confidence ellipse for mean weight and mean girth.

```{r}
# Mean Weight = 95.52, Mean Girth = 93.39
x_b <- c(xbar[1], xbar[4])

# Covariance Matrix of weight and girth
s_weight_girth <- matrix(c(
  3266.46, 1175.50,
  1175.50, 474.98),
  nrow=2, ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)

```

The simultaneous confidence ellipse is given by

$$
(\mu - \bar{x})'S_{WG}^{-1}(\mu - \bar{x}) \leq \frac{\chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}}{n}
$$

```{r}
# chi squared
critical <- qchisq(0.95, df=2)

rhs <- critical/61
rhs
```

or approximately

$$
(\mu - \bar{x})'S_{WG}^{-1}(\mu - \bar{x}) \leq 0.09822073
$$

Explicitly, this is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\mu_W - 95.52 \\
\mu_G - 93.39
\end{bmatrix}^T
\begin{bmatrix}
3266.46 & 1175.50 \\
1175.50 & 474.98
\end{bmatrix}^{-1}
\begin{bmatrix}
\mu_W - 95.52 \\
\mu_G - 93.39
\end{bmatrix} \leq 0.09822073
$$

(c) Obtain the 95% Bonferroni confidence intervals for the six means in part (a).

```{r}
z_bonf <- qnorm(1 - 0.05/(2*6))
z_bonf

margin_bonf <- z_bonf * sqrt(diag(S)/n)

lower_bonf <- xbar - margin_bonf
upper_bonf <- xbar + margin_bonf

bonf_intervals <- cbind(lower_bonf, upper_bonf)
bonf_intervals
```

(d) Refer to part (b). Construct the 95% Bonferroni confidence rectangle for mean weight and
mean girth using m = 6. Compare this rectangle with the simultaneous confidence ellipse
in part (b).

With m = 6, we still use $z^*$ = 2.638257.
Thus, for weight
$$
95.52 \pm 2.638257\sqrt{\frac{3266.46}{61}} \\
76.21406 < \mu_W < 114.82594 \\
$$
and girth
$$
93.39 \pm 2.638257\sqrt{\frac{474.98}{61}} \\
86.02810 < \mu_G < 100.75190 \\
$$

(e) Obtain the 95% Bonferroni confidence interval for (mean head width - mean head length)
using m = 6 + 1 = 7 to allow for this statement as well as statements about each individual
mean.

```{r}
difference <- xbar[6] - xbar[5]

variance <- S[6,6] + S[5,5] - 2*S[6,5]

SE <- sqrt(variance / n)

m <- 7

z <- qnorm(1 - 0.05/(2*m))

lower <- difference - z*SE
upper <- difference + z*SE

c(lower, upper)
```
### 3. Mineral Analysis of Ancient Peruvian Hairs

```{r}
Cr <- c(.48, 40.53, 2.19, .55, .74, .66, .93, .37, .22)

St <- c(12.57, 73.68, 11.13, 20.03, 20.29, .78, 4.64, .43, 1.08)
n = 9

hair <- cbind(Cr, St)

hair
```

(a) Construct and plot a 90% joint confidence ellipse for the population mean vector $\mu^T$ = [$\mu_1$, $\mu_2$], 
assuming these nine hairs represent a random sample from a particular ancient Peruvian culture.

```{r}
x_bar <- colMeans(hair)
x_bar
s <- cov(hair)

critical <- qchisq(0.90, df=2)

dataEllipse(
  hair[,1],
  hair[,2],
  levels = 0.90,
  xlab = "Chromium(ppm)",
  ylab = "Strontium(ppm)"
)
```

(b) Obtain the individual simultaneous 90% confidence intervals for $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ by projecting the
ellipse constructed in part (a) onto each coordinate axis. Does it appear as if this Peruvian
culture has a mean strontium level of 10? That is, are any of the points ($\mu_1$, arbitrary, 10)
in the confidence region? Is [.30, 10]' a plausible value for $\mu$? Discuss.

```{r}
margin <- sqrt(
  qchisq(0.90, df = 2) * diag(s) / n
)

lower <- x_bar - margin
upper <- x_bar + margin

cbind(lower, upper)
```
Yes, it is plausible with a 90% confidence interval that a point exists with strontium = 10 as it is within the interval.
As for [.30, 10],
```{r}
mu0 <- c(0.30,10)

d <- mu0 - x_bar

t <- n * t(d) %*% solve(s) %*% d

t
critical
```
Given that T = 1.772481 < $\chi^2_{2,0.90}$, the point exists within the ellipse and is thus possible.

(c) Do these data appear to be bivariate normal? Discuss their status with reference to Q-Q
plots and a scatter diagram. If the data are not bivariate normal, what implications does
this have for the results in parts (a) and (b)?

```{r}
# Q-Q Plots
qqnorm(Cr, main="Chromium QQ plot")
qqline(Cr)

qqnorm(St, main="Strontium QQ plot")
qqline(St)

# Scatterplot
plot(
  Cr,
  St
)
```
The data does not appear to be bivariate normal with most observations packed to the left and an outlier very far to the right.
This means that the results for (a) and (b) must be treated cautiously as they do not follow the necessary assumptions.

(d) Repeat the analysis with the obvious ”outlying” observation removed. Do the inferences
change? Comment.

```{r}
hair2 <- hair[-2,]
hair2
cat("\n")
n <- 8
xbar2 <- colMeans(hair2)
xbar2
cat("\n")

s2 <- cov(hair2)
s2
cat("\n")

margin <- sqrt(
  qchisq(0.90, df = 2) * diag(s2) / n
)
cat("\n")

lower2 <- xbar2 - margin
upper2 <- xbar2 + margin
cat("\n")

cbind(lower2, upper2)

mu0 <- c(0.30,10)

d <- mu0 - xbar2

t <- n * t(d) %*% solve(s2) %*% d

t
critical

dataEllipse(
  hair2[,1],
  hair2[,2],
  levels = 0.90,
  xlab = "Chromium(ppm)",
  ylab = "Strontium(ppm)"
)
```

Upon removing the outliers, we see changes in the results:
The ellipse is much smaller than previous,
[0.30, 10] is now outside the ellipse with a new t = 5.307872 < 4.60517, the critical value,
10 ppm strontium is also still possible within the 90% confidence interval.

### 4. Lumber Strength Measurements

```{r}
x1 <- c(
  1232,1115,2205,1897,1932,1612,1598,1804,1752,2067,
  2365,1646,1579,1880,1773,
  1712,1932,1820,1900,2426,1558,1470,1858,1587,2208,
  1487,2206,2332,2540,2322
)

x2 <- c(
  4175,6652,7612,10914,10850,7627,6954,8365,9469,6410,
  10327,7320,8196,9709,10370,
  7749,6818,9307,6457,10102,7414,7556,7833,8309,9559,
  6255,10723,5430,12090,10072
)

lumber <- cbind(x1, x2)
```

(a) Construct and sketch a 95% confidence ellipse for the pair [$\mu_1$, $\mu_2$]', where $\mu_1$ = E($X_1$) and
$\mu_2$ = E($X_2$).

```{r}
n <- nrow(lumber)

xbar <- colMeans(lumber)

S <- cov(lumber)

critical <- qchisq(0.95, df = 2)

theta <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 500)

circle <- rbind(cos(theta), sin(theta))

ellipse <- xbar +
  sqrt(critical / n) *
  t(chol(S)) %*% circle

plot(
  x1, x2,
  xlab = "Stiffness",
  ylab = "Bending strength",
  main = "95% Confidence Ellipse"
)

lines(
  ellipse[1,],
  ellipse[2,]
)

points(
  xbar[1],
  xbar[2],
  pch = 19
)
```

(b) Suppose $\mu_10$ = 2,000 and $\mu_20$ = 10,000 represent ”typical” values for stiffness and bending
strength, respectively. Given the result in part (a), are the data consistent with these
values? Explain.

```{r}
mu0 <- c(2000, 10000)

d <- mu0 - xbar

T <- n * t(d) %*% solve(S) %*% d

T
critical
```
Since T = 23.64778 > $\chi^2_{2,0.95}$, then the proposed mean vector (2000, 10000)' is excluded from the 95% confidence ellipse region and is not consistent with the given data.

(c) Is the bivariate normal distribution a viable population model? Explain with reference to Q-Q plots and a scatter diagram.
```{r}
qqnorm(x1)
qqline(x1)

qqnorm(x2)
qqline(x2)

# Scatterplot
plot(
  x1, x2,
  xlab = "Stiffness",
  ylab = "Bending strength",
  main = "Stiffness vs Bending Strength"
)
```
Both Q-Q plots showcase a straight diagonal line consistent with a normal distribution. Furthermore, the scatterplot does appear to have an elliptical shape. However, a sample size of n=30 may not be enough to be entirely conclusive.
